ai.literal: My lord before do not stand, O enemies! Many, my lord before having stood, stone stood.
ai.translation: O enemies, do not stand before my lord! Many who stood before him now stand only as hero-stones.
ai.modern: பகைவர்களே! என் தலைவனுக்கு முன்னால் வந்து நிற்காதீர்கள். என் தலைவனுக்கு முன்னால் வந்து எதிர்த்து நின்ற பலர், இன்று நடுகல்லாகத்தான் நிற்கிறார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet expresses the fierce pride of a warrior boasting about his leader's might. He warns the enemies not to stand in battle against his lord ('என்னை'). The word 'ஐ' here means leader or lord. He reminds them that many brave men who previously dared to stand against his lord were slain and now exist only as 'hero-stones' (நடுகல்) erected in their memory. The play on the word 'stand' (நின்று, நின்றவர்) contrasts standing in battle with standing eternally as a stone monument.

ai.literal: Than the arrow that shot a forest hare, holding a spear that missed an elephant is sweet.
ai.translation: Holding a spear that missed a mighty elephant is far more honorable than holding an arrow that successfully struck down a forest hare.
ai.modern: காட்டு முயலை எய்த அம்பை ஏந்துவதை விட, யானையின் மேல் எறிந்து தவறிய வேலை ஏந்துவது பெருமை தருவதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the virtue of high ambition and courage. The poet contrasts two scenarios: a hunter who successfully shoots a small forest hare with an arrow, and a warrior who hurls a spear at a mighty elephant but misses. Wielding the spear that missed the elephant is considered far more honorable and 'sweet' (இனிது) because it represents a brave attempt at a grand challenge. The contrast between the small 'முயல்' (hare) and the giant 'யானை' (elephant) teaches that aiming high and failing is far more glorious than aiming low and succeeding.

ai.literal: Great valor they say is fearlessness; when one [adversity] occurs, benevolence is indeed its sharp edge.
ai.translation: They say great valor is fearlessness in battle; but when adversity strikes, benevolence toward others is the very sharp edge of that valor.
ai.modern: போர்க்களத்தில் அஞ்சாமல் நிற்பதே சிறந்த ஆண்மை என்று கூறுவர்; ஆனால், பிறருக்குத் துன்பம் வரும்போது அவர்களுக்கு உதவுவதே அந்த ஆண்மையின் கூர்மையான ஆயுதமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true nature of valor (ஆண்மை). While fearlessness (தறுகண்) in the face of danger is considered great valor, it is only half the picture. The poet states that when distress or adversity (ஒன்று உற்றக்கால்) strikes others, showing benevolence and chivalry (ஊராண்மை) is the 'sharp edge' (எஃகு) that perfects and crowns that valor. True strength lies not just in fighting bravely, but in possessing the nobility to help and protect others.

ai.literal: Having thrown the hand-spear at the elephant, he who returns, plucking out the body-spear, smiles.
ai.translation: He who returns after hurling his hand-spear at an elephant smiles with joy as he plucks out another spear lodged in his own body.
ai.modern: தன் கையில் இருந்த வேலை யானையின் மீது எறிந்துவிட்டுத் திரும்புகிறவன், தன் உடம்பில் பாய்ந்திருக்கும் வேலைப் பிடுங்கி மகிழ்ந்து சிரிப்பான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the fierce pride and valor of a classical warrior. Having thrown his only spear to fell a war-elephant, he walks back weaponless. When he realizes an enemy's spear is lodged deep in his own chest or body, he does not lament his wound; instead, he smiles with joy because he has found a new weapon to fight with. The word 'பறியா' shows his eagerness as he plucks the weapon from his own flesh, and 'நகும்' captures his triumphant smile at this discovery.

ai.literal: If the wide-staring eye, when a spear is taken to be thrown, yields and blinks, is that not a defeat to the brave warriors?
ai.translation: If a warrior blinks his wide-staring eyes when an enemy hurls a spear at him, is that momentary blink not a retreat and defeat for his valor?
ai.modern: பகைவன் தன் மேல் வேலை வீசி எறியும்போது, அவனை உற்று நோக்கிய கண்கள் அஞ்சி இமைக்குமானால், அதுவே அந்த வீரனுக்குப் தோல்வி அல்லவா?
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the ultimate standard of military pride and valor. A true warrior keeps his eyes wide open, staring defiantly at the enemy. If he blinks (இமைப்பின்) even for a split second when a spear is thrown at him, that reflex is considered a defeat (ஒட்டு) to his heroic spirit. The word 'அழித்து' here refers to breaking or yielding the steady, fearless gaze of the eye. To the truly brave, even a natural physical reflex of self-defense is seen as a shameful retreat.

ai.literal: Glorious wound not-received days all, among wasted days, he will place, his own days taking and counting.
ai.translation: When a warrior counts the days of his life, he will reckon all those days on which he did not receive a glorious wound in battle as wasted days.
ai.modern: ஒரு வீரன் தன் வாழ்நாட்களைக் கணக்கிட்டுப் பார்க்கும் போது, தன் மார்பில் சிறந்த வீரப்புண் படாத நாட்களை எல்லாம் வீணான நாட்களின் பட்டியலில் சேர்ப்பான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the extreme valor and pride of a warrior. A true hero measures the value of his life not by its length, but by the battles fought and the honorable wounds sustained. When he reviews his past, taking and counting his days, he considers any day without a glorious wound on his chest as a wasted day or a failure. The word 'vazhukku' refers to a slip or fault, here used to mean a day spent in vain without heroic action.

ai.literal: Desiring spreading fame, those who do not desire life, their fastening of the hero's anklet is of the nature of beauty.
ai.translation: For those who desire resounding fame and disregard their own lives, the fastening of the hero's anklet is a fitting ornament of true beauty.
ai.modern: உலகெங்கும் பரவும் புகழை விரும்பி, தம் உயிரைப் பொருட்படுத்தாத வீரர்களுக்கே, காலில் வீரக்கழல் கட்டுவது அழகைத் தரும் தன்மையுடையதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the true meaning of military adornments. The 'kazhal' is a traditional anklet worn by Tamil warriors to symbolize bravery. The poet explains that wearing this anklet is truly beautiful and meaningful only for those brave soldiers who seek resounding fame ('culalum icai') and are willing to sacrifice their lives ('vēṇṭā uyirār') on the battlefield. For anyone else, wearing it would be a hollow gesture without real substance.

ai.literal: When battle occurs, life not-fearing warriors, their king even if angry, glory diminishing they do not have.
ai.translation: Warriors who do not fear for their lives when battle comes will not lose their dignity, even if their king rages against them.
ai.modern: போர் வரும்போது தம் உயிர்க்கு அஞ்சாத வீரர்கள், தம் அரசன் கோபித்துக் கொண்டாலும், தம்முடைய பெருமை குறையப் பெற மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme self-respect and dignity of brave warriors. When battle arrives (உறின்), these soldiers do not fear for their lives (உயிர் அஞ்சா). Their sense of honor is so steadfast that even if their own king or commander becomes angry with them (செறினும்), they will never let their dignity or glory (சீர்) diminish (குன்றல் இலர்). The poet shows that true valor is independent and remains unshaken even by the wrath of one's own ruler.

ai.literal: Those who die without failing what they vowed, who indeed are those who can reprove their failure?
ai.translation: Who is there that can reprove as a failure the death of those heroes who die without failing to fulfill what they vowed?
ai.modern: தாங்கள் சபதம் செய்ததை தவறாமல் நிறைவேற்றுவதற்காக உயிரை விடுபவர்களை, அவர்கள் அடைந்த தோல்விக்காக யாரால் குற்றம் சொல்ல முடியும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet praises the glorious death of warriors who remain true to their vows. When a warrior vows to achieve a heroic deed and dies in the battlefield without retreating or failing his word, his death is a supreme victory of honor. Even if he did not technically achieve the physical objective, no one can mock or reprove him for 'failing,' because he kept his vow unto death. The poet uses the word 'இழைத்தது' to mean 'that which was resolved or vowed' and 'ஒறுக்கிற்பவர்' to mean 'those who can find fault or punish,' highlighting that true honor lies in steadfastness to one's word rather than mere physical survival.

ai.literal: If one dies so that water overflows in the eyes of those who protected them, that death possesses the worthiness of being obtained by begging.
ai.translation: If one can die in such a way that tears well up in the eyes of those who cherished them, such a death is worthy of being sought even by begging.
ai.modern: தம்மைக் காப்பாற்றிய தலைவர்களின் கண்களில் கண்ணீர் பெருகும்படி ஒருவன் இறக்க முடியுமானால், அந்தச் சாவு இரந்து பெற்றுக் கொள்ளத்தக்க தகுதியை உடையதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet extols the ultimate glory of a warrior's death on the battlefield. If a soldier dies fighting so heroically that their commanders or patrons—who nurtured and protected them—shed tears of grief and admiration, that death is the highest honor. The poet suggests that such a meaningful end is so desirable that a warrior should actively beg for it as a boon. The phrase 'புரந்தார்கண் நீர்மல்க' (tears overflowing in the eyes of the protectors) highlights the deep bond of gratitude and duty between the leader and the soldier, making the sacrifice truly noble.
